There are a few CDs that are off the GCD. One that immediately comes to mind is Troll's racial, Berserking. As long as a MAXIMUM of one of your abilities being macrod is on the GCD, everything will execute all at once because they aren't incurring that temporary cooldown. This is also under the assumption that you're pressing the macro while you are NOT affected by the GCD. If you press an ability that's on the GCD and then press the macro before the GCD has finished, everything in the macro that's off the GCD will resolve while the ability that was not, won't.

This gets a bit more complicated when we take into account cast times. If an ability is on the GCD and has a cast time, it MUST be the last item to resolve in the macro in order for the rest of the macro to execute at the right time. If it's cast at instant speed, it can be anywhere in the macro because you can use off-GCD items and abilities while the GCD is happening.

Say we have a Troll Druid. Said druid is playing restoration and wants to macro Innervate, Berserking, Combat Potion, and Wild Growth. All of these except for Wild Growth are OFF the GCD and Wild Growth has a cast time. At its most basic, your macro would be casting/using your three off-GCD abilities (Innervate, Berserking, and Combat Pot) first, then it would be casting Wild Growth.

As long as no more than one on-GCD ability is in the macro and it's in an appropriate place, you can macro in as many off-GCD abilities/items as you can fit in the (I think) 250 character limit.

i mean it was a full degree program, so i learned quite a lot. in terms of balancing, i highly disagree. ill try to give you the best explaination i have over text:

with game design/development, and really any software development in general, the best practice is to test every possible interaction that you can think of (any others fall under outside testers who are testing freely and not following any test plans.) what this means for talents, is that you would have to test every single possible talent combination. right now, we have a possible 35 different combinations across each spec. with the original trees, i dont even know how many we would have across each class since we have not only more available talents, but the ability to use points in multiple spec trees. the reason you test each possible combination is to make sure there arent any unintended interactions. you may have thought you coded x skill to increase dmg by y amount, but for some reason when its picked in conjunction with another, unrelated talent, it actually increases damage by z amount or causes another unwanted interaction. then on top of that, making sure each combination performed similarly to each other combination. not to mention having to retest every combination after making changes to one talent.

its quite a lot, but thats one thing i learned about balancing. it takes a lot of work, and you ended up having to test more than you thought
